statement: In Mila's school, every child who plays in the orchestra also sings in the choir. Tom goes to Mila's school, and he does not sing in the choir. Which of these must be true?

choices.text: Tom does not play in the orchestra.

choices.misconception: I mixed up the two groups and thought that a child who does not sing must play in the orchestra instead.

choices.text: Every child who sings in the choir also plays in the orchestra.
choices.misconception: I turned the rule round: every orchestra player sings, so I thought every singer plays too.

choices.text: Some children who sing in the choir do not play in the orchestra.
choices.misconception: I thought the choir must have singers outside the orchestra, but the rule allows every singer to play as well.

choices.text: Nothing can be said about whether Tom plays in the orchestra.
choices.misconception: I thought the rule only talks about orchestra players, so it says nothing about a child who does not sing.

hints: Imagine Tom were in the orchestra. What would the rule say about him?
The rule says the orchestra sits completely inside the choir. Picture two circles, one inside the other, and decide where a child outside the bigger circle can be.
If Tom played in the orchestra, the rule would make him sing in the choir, but he does not. So he cannot be in the orchestra.

solutions.reliable: Draw the orchestra as a circle inside the bigger circle of the choir, because every orchestra player also sings. Tom is outside the choir circle, so he is outside the orchestra circle too: Tom does not play in the orchestra. The rule does not say every singer plays, so the third statement need not be true, and nothing in it forces the choir to have singers outside the orchestra, so the fourth need not be true either. The transferable idea: 'every A is a B' means anything that is not a B cannot be an A.

whyOnTest: Reading a logical statement precisely: 'every orchestra player sings' does not mean 'every singer plays'.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
